chapter.name: OSPF
chapter.description: OSPF concepts, LSAs, areas, neighbor formation, cost and verification

questions.question: What is OSPF and what algorithm does it use?
questions.answer: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is an open-standard link-state routing protocol (RFC 2328 for v2, RFC 5340 for v3). It floods link-state advertisements and runs the Dijkstra Shortest Path First algorithm to compute loop-free shortest paths.
questions.explanation: Link-state means every router ends up with the same topology map (link-state database) and independently computes routes — fast convergence, no routing loops.
acceptableAnswers: open standard link state protocol using dijkstra spf
hints: Which algorithm name appears in the protocol's full name?

questions.question: What is the default AD of OSPF and what does a route's 'cost' represent?
choices: AD 110; cost based on interface bandwidth (10^8 / bandwidth)
AD 90; cost based on hop count
AD 120; cost based on delay only
questions.answer: AD 110; cost based on interface bandwidth (10^8 / bandwidth)
questions.explanation: Cost = 100,000,000 / bandwidth in bps (e.g. 10 Mb = 10, 100 Mb = 1, Gigabit = 1 on modern IOS which uses a higher reference). Lower total cost = better path.

questions.question: OSPF requires a consistent timer (hello/hold) and network type on both ends of a link to form an adjacency.
questions.explanation: Hello/dead intervals and network type (broadcast vs point-to-point) must match; the router IDs must also be unique. Mismatches leave neighbors in Down/Init/ExStart or flap.

questions.question: Which multicast addresses does OSPFv2 use for hello and LSU packets?
questions.explanation: 224.0.0.5 = AllSPFRouters (hellos, DBDs), 224.0.0.6 = AllDRouters (LSUs sent to the DR/BDR on broadcast segments). RIP uses 224.0.0.9, EIGRP 224.0.0.10.

questions.question: What do LSA types 1, 2, 3 and 5 represent in OSPF?
questions.answer: Type 1 (Router LSA): the router's own links/neighbors, flooded within its area. Type 2 (Network LSA): generated by the DR for a multi-access segment, listing the segment's routers. Type 3 (Summary LSA): a network summarized by the ABR, flooded between areas. Type 5 (AS-External LSA): external routes redistributed into OSPF, flooded everywhere.
questions.explanation: LSA types map to OSPF's link-state database: 1/2 stay inside an area, 3 crosses areas via ABRs, 4 (ASBR summary), 5 external, 7 NSSA-external.
acceptableAnswers: type 1 router lsa, type 2 network lsa by the dr, type 3 summary by abr, type 5 external
hints: Who generates the Network LSA on a broadcast segment?

questions.question: Which LSA type would carry a redistributed EIGRP route into OSPF?
questions.explanation: External routes injected by an ASBR become Type 5 LSAs (or Type 7 in NSSA areas) and are flooded across the OSPF domain.

questions.question: Why does OSPF use areas?
questions.answer: Areas bound the flooding and SPF computation: routers inside an area only run SPF for that area's LSAs, and only summarized information crosses area borders via ABRs. This scales OSPF to large networks.
questions.explanation: Area 0 must be the backbone — every other area must attach to it (physically or via virtual link). All intra-area traffic traverses the backbone.
acceptableAnswers: limits flooding and spf scope for scalability
smaller link state databases per area

questions.question: A non-backbone OSPF area can connect directly to another non-backbone area without passing through Area 0.
questions.explanation: All areas must attach to the backbone (area 0). Two non-backbone areas can only communicate through area 0; a virtual link is the workaround for a disconnected backbone.

questions.question: Enable OSPF on R1 with process ID 1, router ID 1.1.1.1, and advertise network 192.168.10.0/24 into area 0.
questions.explanation: The network statement uses wildcard masks (inverse mask: 0.0.0.255 = /24). The router ID must be unique across the domain. Alternatively use interface mode: `ip ospf 1 area 0`.
hints: The mask in network statements is a wildcard, not a subnet mask.

questions.question: Which command shows the OSPF neighbor table?
questions.explanation: `show ip ospf neighbor` shows neighbor ID, priority, state, dead time and address. Full = adjacency established.
questions.expectedOutput:
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/DR         00:00:37    192.168.10.2    GigabitEthernet0/1

questions.question: Which command shows all OSPF-learned routes (and which routes came from OSPF)?
questions.explanation: `show ip route ospf` filters the routing table to OSPF routes only, showing O and O IA entries. Use `show ip route <prefix>` to inspect a single destination.

questions.question: List the main OSPF neighbor states in order for a broadcast segment.
questions.answer: Down → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full.
questions.explanation: Down: no hellos. Init: hello received from neighbor. 2-Way: bidirectional visibility (DR/BDR election happens here). ExStart/Exchange: database description exchange with master/slave negotiation. Loading: LSR/LSU requests. Full: LSDBs synchronized — adjacency established.
acceptableAnswers: down init 2way exstart exchange loading full
down, init, two-way, exstart, exchange, loading, full

questions.question: Two routers connected over a point-to-point link stay in 2-Way state and never reach Full. What is true?
choices: The adjacency is fully formed — 2-Way is normal on point-to-point links
The link is stuck — 2-Way is not a valid OSPF state
The routers have mismatched area IDs
The DR election failed because both priorities are 0
questions.answer: The adjacency is fully formed — 2-Way is normal on point-to-point links
questions.explanation: On point-to-point links there is no DR/BDR, and neighbors can remain in 2-Way; actual adjacencies typically proceed to Full, but 2-Way on a p2p link is not a failure state by itself. The real 'stuck' states are Init and ExStart.

questions.question: R1 and R2 are directly connected but OSPF shows the neighbor stuck in ExStart/Exchange with constant flap. What is the classic cause?
questions.answer: MTU mismatch: the interface MTU differs between the two ends (e.g. 1500 vs 1492 or 9000), so database description packets larger than the smaller MTU are dropped and the exchange never completes.
questions.explanation: Stuck in ExStart/Exchange with hello working = classic MTU mismatch. Fix by matching MTU or `ip ospf mtu-ignore`. Also check duplex/CRC errors on the link.
acceptableAnswers: mtu mismatch breaks the database exchange
hints: Hellos fit in any MTU; what gets larger during the exchange?

questions.question: OSPF neighbors are in Full, but R2 is not learning R1's network 172.16.1.0/24. What would you check?
symptoms: show ip ospf neighbor shows FULL
questions.answer: Check whether the network was actually advertised: R1's network statement must match the interface (`show run | section router ospf`), the prefix must be in R1's LSDB (`show ip ospf database`), and check for passive-interface on the LAN side — a passive LAN interface sends no hellos (fine) but also must not suppress advertisement; verify the route on R2 with `show ip route ospf` and `show ip ospf database router R1`.
questions.explanation: Full adjacency means hellos work; missing routes mean the prefix was never injected — a missing/mismatched network statement or filter (distribute-list). `show ip ospf database` on the neighbor confirms whether the LSA arrived.
acceptableAnswers: check the network statement and lsa in the database
the prefix was not advertised into ospf
hints: Full state = database sync done. Is the prefix even in the LSDB?

questions.question: What is the OSPF cost of a 100 Mbps interface with the default reference bandwidth?
questions.answer: Cost 1 (100,000,000 / 100,000,000 = 1). With the default reference, 100 Mbps, Gigabit and faster all cost 1 unless the reference is raised with `auto-cost reference-bandwidth`.
questions.explanation: Cost = reference (10^8) / bandwidth. Because 100M, 1G and 10G all give 1, engineers set `auto-cost reference-bandwidth 100000` (100 Gbps reference) or use `ip ospf cost` to discriminate speeds.

questions.question: Raising the OSPF reference bandwidth on one router automatically changes the costs used by its neighbors.
questions.explanation: Cost is a local interface calculation advertised in LSAs. The reference bandwidth must be consistent on ALL routers in the area; otherwise path selection becomes asymmetric/inconsistent.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the DR/BDR on a broadcast (Ethernet) segment?
questions.answer: To reduce the number of adjacencies and the amount of LSU flooding. All routers form full adjacencies only with the DR and BDR, and send their updates to the multicast 224.0.0.6; the DR floods them to everyone. Without DR/BDR, n routers would need n(n-1)/2 full adjacencies.
questions.explanation: Election: highest OSPF priority (default 1) wins; tie → highest router ID. Priority 0 = never elected. DR/BDR elections are per-segment, not per-area.
acceptableAnswers: reduces adjacencies and lsu flooding on broadcast segments
one speaker floods on behalf of all routers
hints: Why does a 20-router Ethernet segment need a speaker?

questions.question: DR election runs on which kinds of OSPF network types?
questions.explanation: DR/BDR exist on multi-access segments (broadcast, NBMA). Point-to-point and point-to-multipoint types never elect a DR.
